templates.pattern: Light travels from medium 1 (refractive index [N1]) into medium 3 (refractive index [N3]) through an intermediate medium. Calculate the effective refractive index from medium 1 to medium 3.
templates.explanation:
Effective refractive index = n₃ ÷ n₁
= [N3] ÷ [N1]
= [RESULT]

The intermediate medium does not affect the overall refractive index ratio. This principle is used in the design of multi-layer optical coatings and fibre optic systems.

templates.pattern: An optical fibre has a core refractive index of [NC] and a cladding refractive index of [NK]. Calculate the sine of the critical angle at the core-cladding boundary.
templates.explanation:
sin C = n_cladding ÷ n_core
= [NK] ÷ [NC]
= [RESULT]

For total internal reflection to occur the angle of incidence inside the core must exceed this critical angle. The core must always have a higher refractive index than the cladding.

templates.pattern: A lens produces an image of height [HI] cm from an object of height [HO] cm. The object is placed [U] cm from the lens. Calculate the magnification of the lens.
templates.explanation:
Magnification = image height ÷ object height
= [HI] ÷ [HO]
= [RESULT]

Magnification can also be calculated as image distance ÷ object distance. Both methods give the same result. A magnification greater than 1 means the image is larger than the object.

templates.pattern: Two thin lenses of focal lengths [F1] cm and [F2] cm are placed in contact. Calculate the total power of the combined lens system in dioptres.
templates.explanation:
Total power = P₁ + P₂
= 100/F₁ + 100/F₂
= 100/[F1] + 100/[F2]
= [100/F1] + [100/F2]
= [RESULT] dioptres

This is equivalent to finding the combined focal length and converting to power. Adding powers is much simpler than adding focal lengths.

templates.pattern: A glass slab of refractive index [N] and thickness [T] cm is placed in the path of a light ray. Calculate the apparent shift of the image produced by the slab in cm.
templates.explanation:
Apparent shift = t × (1 − 1/n)
= [T] × (1 − 1/[N])
= [T] × [1-1/N]
= [RESULT] cm

A glass slab shifts the apparent position of objects behind it toward the observer. The thicker the slab and the higher the refractive index the greater the shift.

templates.pattern: A compound microscope has an objective lens of focal length [FO] cm, an eyepiece of focal length [FE] cm and a tube length of [L] cm. Calculate the total magnification. (near point = 25 cm)
templates.explanation:
Microscope magnification = (L ÷ FO) × (25 ÷ FE)
= ([L] ÷ [FO]) × (25 ÷ [FE])
= [L/FO] × [25/FE]
= [RESULT]×

The objective lens forms a real magnified image. The eyepiece then acts as a magnifying glass to further enlarge this image. The near point of 25 cm is the standard distance for comfortable viewing.

templates.pattern: An astronomical telescope has an objective lens of focal length [FO] cm and an eyepiece of focal length [FE] cm. Calculate the angular magnification in normal adjustment.
templates.explanation:
Angular magnification = FO ÷ FE
= [FO] ÷ [FE]
= [RESULT]×

In normal adjustment the telescope produces an image at infinity. The objective collects light and the eyepiece magnifies the image. A longer objective focal length gives greater magnification.

templates.pattern: In a Young's double slit experiment the slit separation is [d] mm, the screen is [D] m away and the wavelength of light is [LAM] nm. Calculate the fringe spacing in mm.
templates.explanation:
Fringe spacing W = λD ÷ d
= ([LAM] × 10⁻⁹ × [D]) ÷ ([d] × 10⁻³)
= [LAM] × [D] ÷ ([d] × 1000)
= [RESULT] mm

Smaller slit separation produces wider fringes. Longer wavelengths also produce wider fringes. This experiment was the first to demonstrate the wave nature of light.

templates.pattern: In a Young's double slit experiment the fringe spacing is [W] mm, the slit separation is [d] mm and the screen distance is [D] m. Calculate the wavelength of light used in nm.
templates.explanation:
Wavelength λ = W × d ÷ D
= ([W] × 10⁻³ × [d] × 10⁻³) ÷ [D]
= [W] × [d] × 1000 ÷ [D] nm
= [RESULT] nm

Visible light has wavelengths between approximately 400 nm (violet) and 700 nm (red). This experiment can measure wavelengths very accurately.

templates.pattern: An object appears to be at a depth of [AP] cm when viewed through a liquid from directly above. The refractive index of the liquid is [N]. Calculate the real depth of the object in cm.
templates.explanation:
Real depth = apparent depth × refractive index
= [AP] × [N]
= [RESULT] cm

This is the reverse of the apparent depth formula. Objects in denser media appear closer to the surface than they really are because of refraction at the boundary.
